Kurt Vonnegut. The American novelist and social critic whose darkly comic, science-inflected narratives interrogated war, free will, and meaninglessness. Drawing on his experience as a prisoner of war who survived the firebombing of Dresden, he deployed time travel, alien perspectives, and formal experimentation to render catastrophe absorbable and human dignity legible amidst systemic horror. His work blended science fiction, satire, and philosophical rumination into a singular voice. Vonnegut wrote Slaughterhouse-Five in 1969, following Billy Pilgrim, who becomes unstuck in time and witness to the Dresden bombing—fusing autobiography, science fiction, and anti-war polemic. He created Cat's Cradle in 1963, introducing the fictional religion Bokononism and the apocalyptic substance ice-nine, satirizing faith and the hubris of technoscience. Vonnegut authored Breakfast of Champions in 1973, a metafictional collage combining prose, drawings, and postmodern pastiche to explore American violence and consumer culture. Throughout his work, he employed the phrase "So it goes" as a refrain—a mantra of acceptance and darkly comic resignation to death and chaos. He developed an immediately recognizable voice that was colloquial and aphoristic, interrupted by metanarrative asides, oscillating between nihilism and tenderness. His speculative premises, whether time travel, alien contact, or doomsday science, served the psychological and spiritual themes rather than technical novelty.
